# OpenCode vs Claude Code: Harness Differences

Where the two harnesses diverge in ways that change daily workflow. The focus is
the permission interaction, because that is where the gap is widest and least
documented. Mechanism-level detail for OpenCode lives in
[permissions.md](permissions.md) and [skills.md](skills.md); the Claude Code side
of skill execution is in [claude-code/skills.md](../claude-code/skills.md).

> OpenCode docs: [permissions](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/permissions),
> [policies](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/policies),
> [agents](https://opencode.ai/v2/docs/agents).
> Claude Code docs: [permissions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions),
> [permission modes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes),
> [sandboxing](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing).

## Permission interaction

| Aspect | Claude Code | OpenCode V2 |
|--------|-------------|-------------|
| Prompt contents | Human description, the exact command, "This command requires approval", and the exact rule the save option would write (`Yes, and don't ask again for: npm test *`) | Docs define only the decision vocabulary. Prompt contents are client-defined and undocumented |
| Approve with a note | `Tab` on **Yes** opens a comment field; the note is sent to the model after the result | No documented allow-side annotation |
| Deny with a reason | `Tab` on **No** opens a comment field; the note is sent as the denial reason and the model continues | Docs state clients "may attach feedback when rejecting"; no documented TUI affordance |
| Save a rule | "Yes, and don't ask again" saves the pattern named in the option label, and the rule is editable before it is written (`Tab to amend`), then saved to `.claude/settings.local.json`. The save option never accepts a note | "Allow always" saves the pattern the **tool** proposes; the user does not choose, see, or adjust it first |
| Edit rules generally | `/permissions` dialog, listing each rule and its source file | Edit `opencode.json(c)` fragments or the live file by hand |
| Scope of a saved rule | Bash: permanent, per repository and command. File edits: until session end only. WebFetch: per repository and domain | Durable, project-scoped `allow` rules, for every action |
| Rule precedence | `deny` → `ask` → `allow`, first match wins; specificity is irrelevant, and an allow cannot carve an exception out of a broader deny | Last matching rule wins; a narrower exception **must** come later to take effect |
| Modes | Named modes: `default` (Manual), `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions`; `auto` delegates to a classifier model | No permission modes. Agents carry rules; Plan denies edits but not shell |

## What has no OpenCode equivalent

Three gaps that show up every session, in the operator's words:

1. **The prompt does not say clearly what is being asked or what will be granted.**
   Claude's prompt names the action, the exact text to run, and the rule that
   saving would create. OpenCode's documented model is `action` / `resource` /
   `effect`, but the docs never specify what a client renders, and the TUI prompt
   is terse. The rule that "Allow always" writes is chosen by the tool, not shown
   for confirmation.
2. **A decision cannot carry text.** Claude allows a note on either **Yes** or
   **No** on most prompts. OpenCode documents rejection feedback as a client
   capability, with no allow-side equivalent and no confirmed TUI exposure.
3. **"Allow always" cannot be adjusted before it is saved.** In Claude the save
   option embeds the concrete rule and is editable before it is written. In
   OpenCode the pattern is persisted first; adjusting it means editing
   configuration afterwards and, if the file was already reconciled, in both the
   fragment and the live file.

The practical cost is that OpenCode approvals are effectively binary and
optimistic. You grant a pattern you did not author, discover its shape later, and
then prune it manually. Claude's flow lets you inspect and narrow the grant as
part of the approval.

### Caveats on the claims above

- Claude's save-rule options never accept a comment: "The options that allow the
  action for the rest of the session or save a rule don't take one either." A note
  and a saved rule are mutually exclusive there.
- OpenCode prompt rendering is client-specific. The V2 server contract is
  `once` / `always` / `reject`; anything about layout or field visibility is the
  client's choice and may change without a docs update.

## Default posture

Claude Code's Manual mode prompts before edits, shell commands, and most network
access, with a built-in read-only shell allowlist. Recent versions start
interactive sessions in `auto` mode instead, where a classifier reviews actions
rather than the user.

OpenCode is allow-by-default: every agent starts with `{action:"*",
resource:"*", effect:"allow"}`, and only `.env` reads ask. Getting prompt-first
behavior requires an explicit catch-all `ask`. See
[permissions.md](permissions.md#the-catch-all-flip).

## Instructions and skills

| Aspect | Claude Code | OpenCode V2 |
|--------|-------------|-------------|
| Project instruction file | `CLAUDE.md`, or `AGENTS.md` when no `CLAUDE.md` exists | `AGENTS.md` only; `CLAUDE.md` is not read |
| Enforcement | Context only — instructions shape behavior but do not gate tools | Same: instructions are context, permissions are the gate |
| Skill directories | `~/.claude/skills`, `.claude/skills` | Same directories, read in place, plus native and `.agents` roots |
| Skill `!` injection | Expanded before the model sees the skill | Not expanded; literal command text reaches the model |
| Skill and command listings | Skills and commands both surface under `/` | Skills surface under `@`; commands under `/`. Both are listed, under different triggers |
| Auto memory | Yes, per project under `~/.claude/projects/` | No equivalent |

The `!` injection gap is the one that silently breaks migrations: a Claude skill
whose pre-flight never runs still loads cleanly and simply loses its inputs.

## Isolation

Claude Code ships an optional OS-enforced Bash sandbox (off by default) covering
filesystem writes and network egress for shell commands and their descendants.
Deny rules still apply inside it, and it does not cover the built-in file tools,
MCP servers, or hooks.

OpenCode has no built-in sandbox. Permissions match on strings, and shell commands
run with the host user's full filesystem, process, and network authority. The
OpenCode docs say this directly, and recommend a narrow shell allowlist over
patterns that attempt to recognize every dangerous command. Treat OpenCode
permissions as guardrails, not containment.

## Practical implications when migrating

1. Do not assume a Claude `allow` rule and an OpenCode `allow` rule mean the same
   thing: Claude's deny wins regardless of specificity, OpenCode's last match wins.
2. Expect to author saved approvals that OpenCode would have proposed for you.
   Review them after the fact; there is no pre-save editing step.
3. Replace Claude's default-deny posture with an explicit catch-all `ask`. Without
   it, OpenCode stays permissive no matter how many narrow `deny` rules are added.
4. Move any behavior that must not depend on model compliance from instructions
   into permissions or policies. `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md` are both advisory.
5. Budget for the `!` injection gap if you reuse Claude skills, and for
   `CLAUDE.md` not being discovered.
